title: Choosing a career
examples: What if I like art but need a stable job?
How much does my passion affect my salary?
Should I focus on my strengths or what I enjoy?

explain.say: Today we learn about choosing a career path.
First we look at your interests, which are things you enjoy doing.
Next we look at your skills, which are things you are good at doing.

draw.text: Skills: What you are good at

explain.say: Then we look at your values, which are what you think is important in life.
A real life example is planning a volunteer trip abroad.
A good way to learn is by trying out different activities.

items: When: Shadowing day: Observe a job
When: Coursework: Take a short class
When: Volunteering: Help in a new setting

faq.q: Do I need to be perfect at something to choose a career?
faq.a: No, you do not need to be perfect at anything right away. Careers are paths that change as you learn more about yourself.
asks: Can I change my mind about my career?
Is it okay to not know my strengths yet?

faq.q: How much do my interests influence my final job?
faq.a: Your interests guide you toward enjoyable work, but your skills and values must also fit for long-term happiness.
asks: Should I only pick jobs I love?
Are interests more important than skills?

faq.q: What if my skills are different from what I enjoy?
faq.a: You can find roles that use your existing skills while allowing you to develop interests, like data analysis in art.
asks: Can I use my maths skills in a creative job?
Do I have to follow my passions exactly?

faq.q: How do I know what my core values are?
faq.a: Think about what makes you feel proud or what you would fight for. These are often your core values.
asks: What are my most important life goals?
How do I define 'success' for myself?

faq.q: Is it better to study one thing or many things?
faq.a: Studying a range of subjects helps you test many skills and interests before committing to one area.
asks: Should I take many different subjects?
Is breadth better than depth right now?

facts: Interests are activities that naturally capture your attention and curiosity.
Skills are abilities you have developed through practice and learning.
Values are deeply held beliefs about what is important in life, like fairness or security.
Trying out experiences, like shadowing, helps connect interests to real jobs.

quiz.say: A student loves nature and is good at drawing diagrams of plants. Which combination is best?
quiz.why: This combines the interest in nature, the skill in drawing, and the value of contributing to the environment.

wrong.1: This only focuses on the skill of drawing, ignoring the interest in nature.
wrong.2: This focuses on teaching, which might not align with the student's core interest.
wrong.3: This focuses on visual skills but misses the specific connection to the natural world.

quiz.say: If a person values helping others and is skilled at talking to people, which career path might fit?
quiz.why: A counselor uses strong communication skills to help people, matching both the skill and the value.

wrong.0: While it uses problem-solving skills, it might not fulfill the core value of direct human help.
wrong.2: This job uses logic skills but does not strongly align with the value of helping people.
wrong.3: This job uses physical skills but is less focused on interpersonal communication.

quiz.say: Which activity is the best way to test if you enjoy working in an office environment?
quiz.why: Volunteering lets you experience the daily routine of an office without the pressure of a full commitment.

wrong.1: Reading gives information but does not replicate the actual feeling of the environment.
wrong.2: Quizzes can only measure knowledge, not actual practical comfort in a setting.
wrong.3: Talking is good, but seeing it in action is much more reliable for testing comfort.
